utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I understand there are some preliminary matters. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are very short matters. It's really to do with timing. I've had a chance to speak to my learned friend Mr. Lukic, because clearly the Court asked whether it be necessary to sit next week full days. I, for my part, have cut down my cross-examination this afternoon. I would hope that I would be finished by 3.00. But I can't obviously guarantee it, but that's my intention. And I think that Mr. Lukic may have an application that the matter only go as far as evidence-in-chief for the next witness and for cross-examination to be carried over, but he can make that application. But I just give you what my timings will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's always a pleasure for me when Mr. Moore abbreviates or shortens his cross-examination. What I wanted to tell you, based on my conversation with him, and based on what you wanted to hear from me about next week, this is my proposal. If you are leaving it up to me to give a proposal for next day, my proposal is to sit all day on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Friday, and to sit half a day on Monday and Thursday. I think that if we do it this way, then we can, I think, complete three witnesses, especially since one of those three will take a bit longer. So that would be my proposal. Depending on how much time we have left today, after the examination-in-chief of the next witness, I think that you should decide whether we need to proceed with cross-examination of other counsel and so on, and it all depends on when we finish with the current witness. I expect that Mr. Susic, the next witness will take one session in examination-in-chief. So let us see how we proceed and then decide whether we will work full day today or not, and if we sit three full days next week, both morning and in the afternoon, I think we will be right on schedule and we will be able to complete everything. Now, I will leave it up to you to decide whether on Monday and Friday we should sit half days or full days and then the other -- or, rather, on Monday and Friday whether we should sit only in the morning or in the afternoon, but those are the two days that I propose that we work half a day only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm a little confused about Thursday and Friday of next week. I think you said you proposed that we should sit full days Tuesday, Wednesday, and Friday. Did you mean Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Must have been interpretation error. I said Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday. I think that those are the days we can work full day. I don't think anybody feels like working full day on Friday. Unless for some reason we are delayed, then yes, we can sit on Friday full day as well, but I think that everybody would prefer to work fewer hours on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will proceed with the witness and indicate the position. I expect we'll sit Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, full days. The precise hours of sitting we will indicate in due course. The sitting hours on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday next week will be those that we have followed for other full days. That is 9.30 in the morning to 12.45, break for lunch, 2.00 until 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Korica. The affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Mr. Moore is continuing with his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Korica. I have very few questions for you. But I want to deal with two questions that perhaps I should have asked yesterday. The first one was this: You told us that at the hospital you believe that you selected about 20 persons. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: At that time, was Mr. Sljivancanin present within the hospital, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to the meeting, I saw him only once, with the doctors. I didn't see him afterwards until I saw him in front of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could other microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So how long would you estimate that you were at the hospital for before you left? So the time of your arrival until you left, how long?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can be precise about it. We came at around 7.00 and we left the hospital at around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Sljivancanin choose anyone through that period?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where were you going for the selection process, where you found these 20 people? Was that on the basement level? Can you just tell us?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One part was in the rooms, on the ground floor, but also there were some in the corridor, although there were mostly the wounded there. But I think that I took aside very few people there, perhaps two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to ask you a question, it's very difficult to estimate the time, but it's more the topic that will be revealing, and it seems to be somewhere between the early hours of the 20th of November. Were you present when Vujic asked Mr. Kijanovic to go to Velepromet and to check to see if he could find any bodies in Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never heard that. Not even Vujic said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the simple answer is you didn't hear that but you certainly weren't present in any event, if that was said; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to return now to the JNA barracks, on the 20th, and you told us in evidence that Muncan had told you about the troubles at the JNA barracks. I want to deal with that topic. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you ever informed or were you ever told that both Kijanovic and Tomic had approached or gone to Mrksic to tell he, Mrksic, about the trouble at the barracks and indeed that Tomic had likened it to incidents in World War II? Did you ever hear that being said?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything of the sort on the 19th, because we found Mrksic there at that place. Now, as to whether somebody went out with him and told him something there, that's possible, but as long -- as far as I know, and I was present, even though I fell asleep for a while, but while I was present and awake, in my presence nobody approached Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the time when you were at Negoslavci. I'm talking about the period when the JNA barracks, where there was the incident at the JNA barracks, and that the buses had been subject to violence. Talking about the period after that, whether you had heard that Kijanovic and Tomic had left and gone to see Mrksic to express their concerns about what was happening and that Tomic was likening it to a World War II scenario, a bad situation. So that's the period I'm talking about. Did you ever hear that being mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard anybody mentioning anything of the sort, except that Bogdan Vujic said that he had approached Mrksic, and when I asked him when, he said while we were in that room. I didn't see Mrksic, and I said right away that I didn't see Mrksic, and I don't know when he approached him. Nobody else said anything about that. People did talk about incidents, that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal, then, please, with your trip to Ovcara? You went with Muncan in the car and with your other colleagues, that is correct, you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if we try and work out the time, it would appear that you felt it was around dusk, between the light and dark. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you were there, and I know that you said you didn't get out of the car, did you see a digger? When I say a digger, I mean a vehicle that has a large bucket on the front. Did you see a digger present at that time? Can you remember? If you can't, please say so.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember seeing that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal, then, with what you have told us occurred. You remained in the car, and Muncan and his colleague got out but they came back from the Ovcara hangar within five minutes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As far as you could see, is it correct to say that they went inside the hangar at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not able to see the door of the hangar, because it was behind a curve, an angle. However, a policeman stood there. They passed by the policeman, and I suppose they entered but I couldn't see the actual door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: From the conversation that you had with them when they returned, would it be right to say it was your impression that they had looked in to the hangar to assess whether it was possible to carry on with various procedures?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my impression, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When they returned, it's right to say they came back within five minutes, there was no discussion about whether they should try to do anything, it was merely a fact of saying, "There is nothing here for us, the situation for interviews is not appropriate, there is no room, and we will now leave"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muncan only said, "There are no conditions for work here, none whatsoever. There is no light in the room, it's becoming dark, and there is no separate room where we could work." He didn't mention anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about using rooms in the facility apart from the hangar, or trying to find rooms in the facility apart from the hangar?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muncan didn't go looking for that, nor did he inquire with anybody about that. As far as I could see, he went straight back to the car, just as he initially went in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: From your car, how would you -- how far would you estimate it was from your car to the door of the hangar, as you believed it to be?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less than 20 metres. We stopped here, and the door, the entrance to the hangar, was here on this side, and the hangar stretched lengthwise to the left. We stopped in front of the hangar. The policeman was on the corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just imagine your car parked, and you are looking out the front window, was the hangar on the right or on the left?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left from the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, please, to hold up your left arm?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask -- thank you. I'm going to ask that you be given a piece of paper and a pencil, if that's available, and for you to draw the road that you travelled on, the location of the car, and the hangar and where you believed the door would be, and then we will put it on the ELMO. Would you mind doing that now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could you mark the car with an A, please, and the hangar with a B?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The car is pointing to the top of the page, I presume that's the front; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to draw for us what I will call the main road that you travelled on, as best you can? So you have obviously, I presume, a road in front of you and a road behind you. Are you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to put it on the ELMO again, please? So on the left-hand side, we have got the main road going down to Negoslavci, going north, as I call it, going towards Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I drew it all correct, but I think that that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's what you remember; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I remember. I remember travelling that way. I never went there again, so I can't be sure that I drew this correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you remember the hangar on the left?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm going to ask if that could be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit IC 000178, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think perhaps just an exhibit number might do but -- anyway, I'm sure that can be clarified. Perhaps if that could be taken away from the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honours. That will be Exhibit 857.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just deal with literally very few points now. It's right to say that when you were based or when you stopped at Ovcara, from where you were, you could not tell who the territorials were or who the soldiers were. You couldn't distinguish between them. Is that correct? That appeared to be your evidence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said and that's what I think now. I recognised some officers as active-duty officers, what I could see, one or two, and as for others, I couldn't really tell which were members of the TO and which were the JNA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it also, I suggest, flows from your evidence, and indeed I think you said it, that you could not tell whether anybody was the other side off the hangar or how many people were in the hangar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell how many people there were on the other side of the hangar, even though as we were arriving there, we passed through, so perhaps we could have seen whether there was anybody there. But I was unable to see myself whether at the top, towards the top, there was anybody or not because there were soldiers and officers there. And we had come from the lower side; that's how we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see any person blowing a whistle?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I heard it for the first time from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we move on then to your visit to Sid, where I think Mr. Muncan reported to Petkovic? May I deal with that for a moment, please? Am I right in saying that as far as you understood, having spoken to Muncan, that Muncan had the following pieces of information: Firstly, that there had been attacks on the buses in the barracks? Do you accept that? Because it was Muncan who told you about it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muncan told me that there had been attacks by individuals and small groups on buses, but he didn't tell me that there was any physical fight because people had already been on the buses, and those other ones did not enter buses, nor did they, as far as I could hear, break the windows or do anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The second piece of information that he had was that he had been to the Ovcara hangar, because you've given evidence of that. That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly informed him of that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And thirdly, Muncan may well have been able to inform Petkovic of anything that you had told he, Muncan; that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could tell about what happened in the hospital. As for Velepromet, he was there himself, and there was no need for me to inform him of anything because he was able to see it for himself. As for what took place in the hospital, he must have informed him about that but there was nothing of interest, and everything concluded the way we had foreseen and planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did Muncan tell you, in general terms, what he had reported to Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not give me any details. We did talk about it, that he reported to Petkovic about everything that had happened over those two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: After you had reported to Petkovic, where did you go, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three of us went to the apartment immediately, and Muncan went to Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when he returned from Petkovic, where were you, and where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in this private apartment near the post office where we had been earlier and we were there then too. We were there for about 20 days altogether.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones please be switched off when the witness speaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think you told us that you had not had sleep for two days; is that right, by the end of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that when you went to the apartment, you had a well-deserved sleep?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I had a beer and then I went to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you report to Petkovic the following day?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never reported to Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So it would be right to say that you would not be able to say if Vujic had given a report to Petkovic on the 21st. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You remember giving evidence about your friends teasing you about being Bogdan Vujic's security?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you have told us that Vujic had made a suggestion in his statement that you had a gun on your knee. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that in his statement that he gave to the investigator from The Hague, the first statement he gave, in his apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Forgive me asking this question. I don't mean to be insensitive. You have told us that you are a widower. When did your wife die, please, which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When Vujic showed you this statement, was it before or after your wife's death?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I read to you from Vujic's statement that he gave to the OTP? And this is the only statement that he gave to the OTP. To assist my learned friends, it's paragraph 51. It's English 26 of 40. I'm just going to read a small part. "On my return to the Velepromet at about 10.30 or 11.00, I met Branko Korica in the office of Captain First Class Borisavljevic as agreed. In the room there was another captain armed with a semi-automatic machine-gun standing next to the telephone on which he spoke several times but I don't know to whom." That is the only reference to a gun that involves you or is close to your name, and it is attributed to another person, not you. Might I suggest you have -- might have made a mistake on that point?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. I read that too. I read it myself. Now, whether he gave this, he said that he gave this statement to the investigator from The Hague, but I don't know who he gave statements to, all these people, to the military court, the special court, the investigator from The Hague. But I read what he said, where he says, "When I first came to Velepromet I found Branko Korica sitting there in an armchair with a rifle on his knees." I am sorry but this is literally what I said to him, "Comrade Colonel, are you crazy? I never had a long weapon in my hands." No rifle. I can prove that. I never had that. You can see in the passes -- my passes that I had there. Bogdan Vujic, if he stated that, he didn't find me in an office with some captain who I had never seen. We came together from the hospital to Velepromet at this hour that he referred to, that is correct, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, all I'm suggesting to you is that there is no reference in the one statement that he made for the Office of the Prosecutor to you having a gun. So I just suggest that to you in fairness. You have also said that Mr. Vujic, Bogdan Vujic, referred to buses and had asked you about how many buses there were. Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that, that he asked me that. He asked me in the street. "Do you know how many buses there were when we were taking those people out?" And I said, "I have no idea where the buses were." And he said, "Well, out there behind the barracks, how many were there?" And I said, "I have no idea." That's the only thing he asked me about the buses and that was the only answer I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that, as far as you can recollect, was one year after you had been to Vukovar. That is right, isn't it? That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, a year me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I seem to remember from your evidence that you remained in the Vukovar area until approximately the 15th of March, 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What was your task throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were going around Vukovar, we were going around the entire territory. We conducted interviews with many persons. We found many documents. I have already mentioned that notebook concerning minefields. That's how we found other reports of the military police of the Croatian army, where it says report of the military police, number 16, such and such a date, number 1, arrested because he was a Serb, because he has zero blood group, RH negative, consult Vesna Bosanac and so on and so forth, why they were arrested and so on. There were quite a few documents of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. You told us that, and I quote, you don't have such a good name -- such a good head for names. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You were at Velepromet for three hours basically on the night of the 19th, and you stayed with Vujic principally on the 20 at Velepromet. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could you just help me in one matter? Why is it through your evidence, on at least two occasions, you referred to the head of the TO by his Christian name, Ljubinko, as opposed to his surname? Did you get to know him in the three-month period?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We called him Ljubinko, and I wasn't sure whether his last name was Stojic or Stojanovic. However, we all addressed him as Ljubinko. I knew him as Ljubinko, and I saw that he played the main role in Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that you spoke to him after the 20th of November in the period that you remained there, up until March 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't talk to Ljubinko anymore. I talked more at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the use of the Christian name to Ljubinko was because of your contact with him on the evening of the 19th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th and on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When did you meet him on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw him before the government meeting, because Vujic and I came and we walked around the compound and went back to the office. I think Ljubinko was in this other office. I saw him go there but we didn't talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if you didn't talk to him, you wouldn't have been calling him by his name, would you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called him by his first name because we talked quite a bit on the previous day, and because he intervened there while Vujic held this meeting with the others in an office. He needed some vehicle. His friend got killed, I know he was shouting there, saying something, "You are holding these meetings and I haven't got a vehicle for my friend."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What do you mean about his friend got killed and he was shouting something? When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened when we arrived in Velepromet and while Vujic had this meeting with the others in the office. I was not at that meeting. I was outside. That's how I saw him intervene. He said, "Where are these people?" And somebody said, "At the meeting." And then he barged in through the door and then he started shouting from the door, saying, "You are holding these meetings here, and my friend got killed and I need a vehicle." And that's why the meeting ended sooner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You say that you had dealings with Mr. Basic. Were you aware that in a report that he submitted that he indicated in that report that there was liquidation of Croat populations by Chetniks and members of the Seselj group? Were you aware of that in your period in Vukovar until March?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dealing with the radio that you found through that period, it is right to say that the radio was not in the hospital but was beside a watchmaker's in a built-up area close to the hospital. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This radio was opposite the hospital, across the street. It wasn't in the hospital. It was across the street in a completely different row of houses, in a yard, next door to the watchmaker's shop. That was the area that had been mined but we didn't know. We discovered it only the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Various people from the Office of the Prosecutor, including myself, came to Belgrade in the middle of September of this -- of this year because summonses had been issued. Now, there were four summonses issued. One was for Mr. Susic, who will be giving evidence; Mr. Kijanovic, who came to OTP office and signed a statement, he will be giving evidence; and Mr. Karanfilov will be giving evidence. And they all came to see the people there. There was a summons issued for you. Did you receive that summons?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never got the summons. I never heard of the summons being sent to me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge of the summons being given to your son to give to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that but I believe that my son would have told me. I don't believe that the summons was handed to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you in Belgrade between the 15th and the 18th of September of this year?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the 15th and the 18th of September? No. I was at my weekend cottage in Novi Slankamen. That's 50 kilometres away from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I suggest the following to you, or perhaps there should be one more question. How were you contacted by the Defence team of Mr. Sljivancanin? Was that through official channels?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Lukic called me on the telephone, and he asked whether we could see each other in relation to giving evidence. I said that we could when I come to Belgrade. Since he was spending very few days in Belgrade, I came to his office the very next day and that's when we talked for the first time. It wasn't anything official. Nothing was being written down. I did not give any statement. Mr. Lukic sort of took some notes but nothing official.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you explained to Mr. Lukic what it was you remembered; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes, in brief terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how long did that interview or conversation last?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did he refer back to you about the topics under discussion, to make sure that he had got it accurately?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't take me back to anything, but he mentioned to me the possibility that I might testify before the Court, and I said, "If at all possible, try to skip me. I like it better being at my weekend cottage." But then he called me again and he says, "Well, it seems to me you'll have to go."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you have any objection to showing the Office of the Prosecutor the document that was created from the information you gave?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I suggest to you the following. I would suggest to you that at Velepromet, when you arrived, that Mr. Sljivancanin did make a comment about possible killings in Velepromet, but I think it's right to say you don't agree. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would equally suggest to you that at Velepromet, there was what I will call perceptible violence which Vujic tried to stop and you were aware of that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to go back to that other thing. You said Sljivancanin, Velepromet; no, no. I never saw Sljivancanin in Velepromet. As for violence, the violence that was there, I did not understand it that way, to be that kind of violence, as Vujic presented it, the use of the BOV and whatever, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: At the hospital, I suggest that in actual fact Vujic did not participate in this selection procedure, as you say.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he did but I know that he took people out, just like I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And finally this: Did you know a gentleman called Colonel Panic, who was the Chief of Staff of OG South at that time? Did you know his name or were you able to recognise him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know of Panic then, nor do I remember having seen him. Perhaps we did come across each other but I don't remember at all. I saw Panic now, the one that you're asking me about, but I really do not remember having seen him anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And finally, I would suggest that there were threats against Vujic being made at Velepromet and threats of severe violence to him. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They talked about that to me. They threatened me as well. However, we talked, we went next to each other. We stood shoulder to shoulder, walking around Velepromet compound when this was happening. Nobody pulled us by the arm or anything like that. Those were the threats. That was the essence of the threats addressed to us, that we were protecting Ustashas. They were angry at us. They said, "You officers don't know what they did." And we said, "Yes, we know what they did."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the last sentence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the essence of those threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the interpreter didn't hear the last part of your evidence. Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there was no serious threat towards myself. And as for Vujic, I don't know what happened when I wasn't with him. I don't know what kind of things they told him when I wasn't with him. But at the time, when I was with him, it didn't happen. Nor did Vujic complain to me about that, nor did I tell him anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Lukic. Re-examination by Lukic:

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Korica, would you like to have a break or would you rather begin? I don't have long. Let me tell you that straight.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Very well. Let us first start with the questions that Mr. Moore put to you. I'd like to clarify some of the issues raised by Mr. Moore and Mr. Vasic. Do you remember by any chance when was the first time I contacted you? How long ago was that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. Perhaps more than a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The sentence concerning Chetniks slaughtering and Velepromet, when was the first time I asked you that? Do you remember? What type of a meeting and a conversation did we have? Did we meet?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You called me on the telephone but I don't remember now when that was. I can't even give you a rough idea. It seems to me that it was only month and a half ago, but if I put things in perspective and remember what I did when I did, then it must have been prior to that, but I can't tell you how long prior to that. You called me on the phone and you asked me this: Is it true that in Negoslavci, in the office where we were, Mr. Sljivancanin said that we would see how Chetniks slaughter Ustashas but that we should disregard it, we should not pay attention to it? I heard no such sentence and I don't know when he could have uttered it. Sljivancanin was with us for five minutes alone and we were there in a relatively small area, so I didn't hear this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. I raised this with you during examination-in-chief but let us cover this ground again. Were you with Mr. Vujic there when he talked to Sljivancanin? It's a relatively small room.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was always right next to me. He always stood right next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Moore asked you whether your son might have received some kind of a summons. Would you please tell Their Honours this: While you were in your small -- in your weekend house, did somebody come to your apartment? Did somebody come to your apartment and ask for something, insist on something?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a girl who lives in my apartment. She lives there and cleans the apartment. I also have a lady neighbour, and I'm on very good terms with her. Since you had told me that there was a chance that I would come and testify here, I asked these two women to go to my mail box every day and check it, or if somebody called me on the phone, that they should tell that person where I was; namely, at my weekend cottage. However, nobody looked for me. Nobody came to the apartment looking for me. Nor did anybody send any kind of a summons. I heard this later on, and it was quite unpleasant, not only to me but to my entire family, namely police came looking for me and it was the police from Indjija. They didn't come to my weekend cottage in Slankamen. Rather, they came to Cortanovci, which is a place near Novi Sad, and they also looked for me in some other villages. They came across a relative of mine whose son had been killed in this war and she got scared, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. At any rate, the police came looking for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an intervention for the transcript, page 22, line 9, the witness said: "We were in a small area, and God forbid that I should have heard everything else but that." That's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please turn off his microphone when the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You drew a sketch of the area in front of the hangar and the road that you took to the hangar. How long did you spend that day at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven to eight, maximum ten minutes altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever go back to Ovcara ever again?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that that was around dusk. We don't need to elaborate on that. You said to Mr. Moore that it was difficult to discern the uniforms, whether these people were members of the TO or soldiers, as you were describing what you saw in front of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and observing it from the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: At the entrance into the hangar, the people who stood there, what kind of insignia did they have?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were from the military police. One was a military policeman and further from him there stood another two military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore also asked you about Ljubinko Stojanovic. You said that you saw him twice and he asked you how come you knew his first name. My question: Throughout the three months that you stayed at Vukovar, did you hear his name? Was he an important person there? Was his name mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that he was a relevant person in Velepromet. He was important there. And as for Vukovar, when we contacted people, for example, in the hospital, in the staffs of local communes and so on, nobody mentioned him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us go back to the questions that were raised yesterday. On page 14787, I'm giving this reference for the Trial Chamber, Mr. Moore suggested to you that pursuant to the instructions you had received from Babic, you had no command responsibility and you confirmed that. Now let me ask you this: What are the relations between security organs at different levels, given that you spent a lot of your work for many years in that area?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to professional issues, then, yes. And as for disciplinary issues, then they report to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. When Babic told you to put on your uniform again, what was your status in the JNA? Were you considered a reserve officer at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a reserve non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see Exhibit 107, which are the rules of service of the security organs, Article 14; English version page 9, and B/C/S version page 8. Could that be please placed in front of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You will see it on the screen, Mr. Korica. I suppose that you remember this document. This was something you were all very familiar with. I'm reading Article 14: "Members of security organs from the reserve strength of the armed forces, when called up for exercises, or verify combat readiness and other activity in combat units of the armed forces and perform tasks within the competence of the security organs in accordance with the regulations on the work of security organs." Did I read this out correctly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you were told to put on your uniform, were you able to refuse? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had that been ordered to me, I would have been unable to refuse. However, this was under different circumstances. This was just a simple conversation. But I took it seriously so there was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters for not switching my microphone off. I hear that there are problems with that. Who was your immediate superior in Sid?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Muncan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Who was his immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Ljubisa Petkovic. He's now deceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you happen to know who was immediate superior to Tomic, Kijanovic and Vujic? Do you know that? Before they arrived in Sid, from wherever they had arrived?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they had arrived from, and I don't know who their superior was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a bit earlier to Mr. Moore that Muncan told you that he had reported to Petkovic upon his arrival in Sid.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before arriving in Sid, did Muncan submit any kind of report to anyone in the course of those two days? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, and I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. When you left from Velepromet, heading towards Ovcara and then further on to Sid, did you report to anyone saying, "We are on our way to Ovcara now" or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Muncan contacted anyone in the barracks telling them that he would go to Ovcara as well. I don't know about that. He didn't tell us anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you didn't go to Negoslavci; that's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't go to Negoslavci at all. We went straight to Sid, and we didn't meet with this group consisting of Vujic, Kijanovic and Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you said twice, first to Vasic and then on page 7 of the draft transcript, and then to Mr. Moore on page 42, that both in Velepromet and at the hospital your immediate superior was Bogdan Vujic. Remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Then on page 44, Mr. Moore asked you whether, when Sljivancanin told you in the car on the way to the hospital about the upcoming activities, you said that it was in the form of a proposal, a suggestion, and when the Prosecutor asked you whether an order and a proposal have the same effect, you answered yes. I just gave you this in order to remind you of it. My question to you is: How long did you spend in the army, Mr. Korica?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, no, no. Just tell me first how long did you spend in the army.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 33 years altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: During the 33 years of your service in the army, did you ever hear that a major ordered something to a colonel?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: During the 33 years of your service in the army, did you ever hear a major propose something to a colonel?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Let us proceed. Yesterday Mr. Moore put to you statements of various persons describing terrible things from Velepromet, the stories that they told here, which, according to their evidence, happened perhaps not at the same time but the same evening when you arrived. During the course of that evening, did you hear from anyone in Velepromet stories about something of that sort happening prior to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I neither heard nor saw traces of any such crime. I don't know whether it did take place indeed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The persons whose name you wrote down in the buses - I guess you went from one to the other one and then wrote down their buses - did you observe on any one of them, any injuries, anything that would indicate that force had been used?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anything, not in relation to a single person. Didn't see a single scratch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What was their mood like? You are a professional, after all. You can certainly sense when a person is experiencing fear, when a person is intimidated, anxious or anything of the sort. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember. I looked all of them in the eye. What can I tell you? People are different. Some people sat there, they were relaxed, they gave me their particulars without any problem. And then there were people who were tense. It was an unpleasant atmosphere but what could we do about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore, on page 73 of the draft transcript asked you yesterday about your return from Velepromet to Negoslavci. You said that you went to have a dinner briefly and then returned to the operations room where you stayed until the following morning. My question is: While you ate in that basement, where was Bogdan Vujic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think that he was in the basement as well, and that he opened a can, too, but my memory is not quite clear on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that basement? Could you estimate?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Half an hour at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the rest of time you were upstairs in that operations room; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long did you sleep that night?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I slept more than an hour, because at one point I fell asleep and then I woke up and I saw General Crmaric next to me and then I started talking to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: At any point in time, ever since you walked into that command building in Negoslavci, until the next morning, when you went to the hospital, did you ever see Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I'm not sure that I saw Colonel Mrksic either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You were asked about making these lists, and you described the first evening in Velepromet and then the next day in the hospital. Can you remind us what time of day was it when you were making lists in Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were making lists in Velepromet, it was, I think, after 11.00, around midnight almost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that you think that you left the hospital around 10.00 on the next day.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said. As for time, I cannot say --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It will mean something to us. It will help all the participants in the proceedings. Do you remember yesterday, did you see Sljivancanin in the hospital at one moment talking to the representatives of the international community?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that that will be sufficient for all of us so that we can focus in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please switch off his microphone when the witness is speaking, asks the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now I'm talking about the 20th, the triage. Did you hear Vujic asking for lists to be made of the persons who are taken out?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't ask for a list to be made and he didn't make them either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have one more topic to deal with, and it's the briefcase that you talked about. We all heard Mr. Vujic's testimony and you read his statement. That's what you said. You said that you were familiar with the statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: On page 4545, Your Honours. Let me ask you first, what did you do with the briefcase ultimately?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I did not see Vujic anymore that day, I stayed in Velepromet. I was picked up by Muncan, we went to Ovcara and directly to Sid, and they stayed on in the barracks, so I did not hand that briefcase over to the police immediately. It remained with me. I took it to Sid. Two or three days later, I went to Sremska Mitrovica, and I took this briefcase, and although it was in the evening, I looked for Bogdan Vujic, found him, gave him that briefcase and asked him to see what this group of prisoners -- or, rather, these people who were brought in on those four buses to see whether these people were perhaps there and to have this handed over to them and, if not, to send it or to take it to the security administration and that is indeed what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When Mr. Vujic testified here, as I said, on page 4545, and in his statement given to the OTP that he said that he showed to you, he mentions that in this briefcase there was an ID and other documents with the name of Vladomir Vodopija. You said you were not very good with names, but does this jog your memory? Is that perhaps one of the names that you found in this document, Vodopija Vladomir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. But Vujic did not even look at the bag, not -- he didn't look at a single one of the documents that I was writing down. Now, whether he did that in Sremska Mitrovica, if he did that in Sremska Mitrovica opened the bag then he certainly could have remembered that name but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we now please have the following document placed on the screen? 2D 050049, the lists of prisoners in the Sremska Mitrovica prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an official document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't quite follow how this arises out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Moore focused on the briefcase and the documents in the briefcase for quite a while, and whether these persons were persons who had been killed. Those were his questions. Now I would just like to show the witness a document where this -- where one of these people was, one of the persons whose documents were in that briefcase, because he said that he took the briefcase to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't yet see how that's going to be a matter arising from cross-examination. There was certainly question about the contents of the briefcase, and they were identified, but nobody went into any identifications of anybody. It was merely a briefcase with certain contents. They were identified by the witness on his own notes, and he then was to deliver them to Belgrade I think was all that was dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I find the relevant transcript page, Your Honour? The core of Mr. Moore's question was what did Borisavljevic say, where was the bag found? And the witness said it was -- that he heard that it was found behind the hangar, and then Mr. Moore asked the witness whether it was possible that these persons whose IDs were found had been killed. That's the subject. And that is why I'm dealing with it in redirect, since the witness took the bag to Sremska Mitrovica, whether he knows the name of the person whose ID was taken in the bag to Sremska Mitrovica. That is the subject. Vujic testified about that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There was a speculative question about who the possible owners might be. Now, how does what you are doing arise from that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you remember, Mr. Korica, when he was giving his answer to that question of Mr. Moore's he said, first of all, that he thinks that at that time documents were taken away from people at check-points. He heard about that. And that they had information about these documents who were taken away from people although these people survived, because Mr. Moore asked whether it was possible that these persons had been killed. And the witness said that it was his own experience that sometimes people's documents were simply taken away from them. I am dealing with this now because -- I don't want to say too much in front of the witness, but he asked just to see whether the man is alive, the man whose ID was in that bag. That is what stems from those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's come sufficiently clear to me, Mr. Lukic, that you may go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise once again. My train of thought, it seems to be too complicated, but could we please have the document on the screen, 2D 050049.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: See, Mr. Korica, can you read the name under 1563, what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vladomir Vodopija. Probably his father's name is Ivan, 16/12/44.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please turn off his microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this moved to the left a bit, please, although probably this won't mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Actually, can you say in view of your own experience what this next thing should be?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KORICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personal identification number probably.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure, but it seems to me that all the lists of prisoners in Sremska Mitrovica have already become an exhibit, but I'm not sure. I tried to check this with my associates, but if not, then I would like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there is another leap that I have missed. On what basis do you say this is presently admissible?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the witness whether he remembered whether this refreshes his memory, when he looked at that briefcase, whether he finds this name Vladomir Vodopija to be familiar as one of the people whose ID was in that bag, and the witness said that it was possible. I asked him in the beginning. But at first, Your Honour, Mr. Vujic testified about that on page 4545, and he said that this man had been director of the waterworks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Any submission, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My recollection is that my learned friend is right about the head of the waterworks in Vukovar. But I do not remember this being put to Mr. Vujic, what he had done with the document, whether he ever got the document, and whether this process was followed with Mr. Vujic. I could see it being admissible arguably in relation to that witness, but not with regard to this witness, because it has a basis of speculation, of what is capable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document will be received, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 858, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But don't get over-enthusiastic about what you have managed because we see a number of factual difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, it's my fault. I thought Your Honour was asking in relation to the nature of the question. The document itself, I for my part cannot remember the provenance of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are conscious of that and that was part of the reason for my last cautionary words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I respectfully submit for it to be marked for identification until such time as we clarify exactly what the provenance is? I'm sorry for not submitting it earlier. I thought Your Honour was asking in relation to the other matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment you dispute the provenance of the document. Is that the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to see what the provenance is before I even dispute it. I don't dispute just for the sake of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance? This is an official document of the government of the Republic of Croatia submitted to us by the OTP. I think that the document has about 20 pages, and I think that it followed the documentation of Mr. Grujic about those camps where Croats were detained, but this was part of his expertise. One page of this document, I think, we admitted into evidence as P030, and it was Exhibit 273. Or, rather, 133. Exhibit 133 and Exhibit 273. See how many people I have working with me? These are parts of this big list that we showed witnesses earlier on and they were admitted into evidence. It's a long list. It has to do with prisoners who were in prison in Sremska Mitrovica from Vukovar. There are others, too, prison in Valjevo, there are quite a few correctional facilities referred to. But what I referred to just now are two exhibits with identical details concerning other persons. Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions of this witness. I don't know whether this has been sufficient to remind Mr. Moore of these documents, what I said just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document has been admitted as exhibit. There will be leave to Mr. Moore to raise objections to the provenance of that admission, should he wish to bring the matter forward. Mr. Korica, you'll be pleased to know that in the middle of all of that, we came to the end of your evidence. Mr. Lukic has no further questions, and we would like to thank you for coming to The Hague and for the assistance that you have given us. And you are now free, of course, to go back to your home and your other interests. Thank you very much indeed. The court officer will show you out when we rise. We will now adjourn and will resume at a quarter past.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Bulatovic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Susic. For the sake of the quality of the interpretation of our exchanges here, I would like to kindly ask you to make a pause after hearing my question before proceeding with your answer, and then to speak slowly so that the interpreters can interpret what you are saying. Did you understand?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, would you please give us your full name, last name, date and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Jovan Susic, born on the 13th of April, 1957, in the village of Bukovica, Savnik municipality, Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, we are now going to cover your military career and if you can just confirm to me whether what I'm saying is correct. Is it true that currently and starting from 2004, you have been holding the position of a chief within the Ministry of the Defence of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I now worked in the inspectorate of the Ministry of Defence, as a chief there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: As a chief there, all right. In 1989, you completed the military academy, department for land forces?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: From 1985 to 1989, you were commander of a military police company within the Guards Brigade. What years?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: It was 1982 to 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In that case I got it wrong, I noted it down wrong, when we talked.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: And I completed my military academy in 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And then from 1991 to 1994, you were commander of the 1st Battalion of the military police within the Guards Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Starting in this 1994 to 1996, you attended training within the military staff academy?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Then for two years, you served as battalion commander of military police for anti-terrorist activity of the 72nd Brigade --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: -- from 1996 to 1998. And then in 2000 and 2001, you once again attended training at the national school for defence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And then you became chief of the department for operations and planning within the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And we know about your current position. What's your rank?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, we are now going to turn to the events in Vukovar and to some key days that will be of interest to all of us here. Do you know what position you held immediately before the Guards Brigade was deployed to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Immediately before the Guards Brigade left Vukovar, I was deputy commander of the 1st Battalion of military police of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, would you please slow down for the sake of interpretation. Can you explain to us when you went to Vukovar and whether you were immediately involved in any operations?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: We went to Vukovar on the 30th of September, 1991. Our battalion was tasked with providing security to the Guards Brigade on its march from Belgrade to Negoslavci. Further on, to provide security to the units in -- until they reached their area of deployment and then to provide security to the command of the Guards Brigade, as well as to various transports and columns.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, where was the headquarters of the Guards Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: In the village of Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, can you tell us something about the composition, establishment composition of the 1st Battalion of military police?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: The composition of the 1st Military Police Battalion comprised the command, signals section, crime section, section for sabotage protection, the 1st Company of armoured vehicles, the 2nd Company of armoured vehicles, military police company, anti-terrorist company of military police, traffic company of military police, logistics platoon, and a special auto platoon which was not involved in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell me, please, the 1st Military Police Battalion, did it come to Vukovar with full strength, establishment strength?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did, except for the special auto platoon which was not engaged in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that within the composition of the 1st Military Police Battalion there were two companies of armoured vehicles. Would you give us names of commanders of those companies?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Commander of the 1st Company of armoured vehicles was Lieutenant Ranko Bojic, and the second one was commanded by Captain Mladen Predojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who was assistant for moral guidance in the 1st Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Assistant for moral guidance was Captain Bozic, Mile.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you came to be appointed commander of the 1st Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I became commander of the 1st Military Police Battalion on the 1st of November, 1991, due to the illness of the commander, Major Branislav Kavalic, who was sent for treatment to the military medical academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, would you please slow down so that the interpreters can be sure to catch everything you say. You said something initially and I would like to clarify this. Upon your arrival in Vukovar, what were the tasks of the 1st Military Police Battalion, the tasks of the battalion as well as the units within its establishment composition. Slowly and clearly, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Upon arrival in Negoslavci, the task of the battalion was to provide security to the command of the Guards Brigade. In addition, it was to escort the column from Belgrade to Negoslavci and back. Also to provide traffic, security of the logistics -- or, rather, rear command post of the brigade which was located in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did the 1st Military Police Battalion have its own command?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did, in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, intervention for the transcript. I think the interpreters didn't hear the answer concerning the rear command post of the Guards Brigade, secured by the 1st Military Police Battalion so could the witness please repeat where was the rear command post of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, please wait for me to complete my question and then slowly proceed with your answer. Would you please tell us where the rear command post was?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: The rear command post of the Guards Brigade was in Berak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you were appointed commander of the 1st Military Police Battalion, where was your command post?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: My command post was also located in Negoslavci, but our forward command post was in the barracks in Vukovar, and this is where I was the entire time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain, Mr. Susic, why this forward command post existed in the barracks and why did you spend time there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: The forward command post existed within the command because after the first, the anti-terrorist company was deployed back to combat on the axis Rusinska-Crkva, fire brigade, Supanc school, water-tower, between the 1st and 2nd Assault Detachments. Due to this, it was necessary to have a command post that would be located closer to the combat unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, could you please explain the chain of command within the 1st Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Within the 1st Military Police Battalion, the chain of command went from the commander towards company commanders and from them towards platoon commanders. As for myself, as commander I received my tasks from the commander of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the commander of the Guards Brigade, did you receive any additional orders or tasks from any other officer?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I could not receive orders from anyone else but the commander of the Guards Brigade. It wasn't typical for anyone to interfere in the command process.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The tasks you received from the commander of the Guards Brigade, how did you receive them, orally, in writing? Would you please explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: We received the tasks from the commander both verbally, in writing, and via telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do upon receiving a task? Did you proceed, based on that task?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: When one receives a task from the commander, then one proceeds with its implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The means of implementing a task, did you work on it yourself, with whom, and how?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. We analysed and worked on the task with the forces that were supposed to implement it. First with the command of the 1st Military Battalion and then with the commanders of various companies and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any briefings in the command of the Guards Brigade and, if so, when were they held? Was it on a daily basis? I'm interested also in the time of the day, and would you please explain to us the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Briefings were held daily at 1800 hours at the command of the brigade -- at the command post of the brigade. Briefings were attended by the commander, assistant commanders, and battalion commanders. First commander would brief or, rather, describe certain activities; and then later on, battalion commanders informed about their positions, any requirements that they had and so on. These briefings lasted from one to two hours approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can we turn into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, this task, on the 18th, for part of this company, you said was issued by the commander of the Guards Brigade, Mrksic. Can you describe how come you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: When Captain Maric was given the task of going to Ovcara and to check what the accommodation of the prisoners from the Mitnica Battalion was like, he informed me that this was a task that he had received from Commander Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was this the usual way of command?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No. It is not the usual one but it is possible to handle things that way. The commander, as in komandant, can issue tasks to the commander, as in komandir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In a commander who is not the immediate superior issues a task, what does the subordinate person do?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Since I did not issue that order to him, Maric reported to me that he was given this task by the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, on the 18th, the date you remember as the date of the fall of Vukovar, did you perhaps have some other tasks or not? Any particular tasks?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: No particular tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: A few moments ago you spoke about the briefings that were held around 1800 hours in Negoslavci, as you said, and you said that you attended these briefings. Do you remember whether you were there on the 19th of November, 1991 at the briefing at the command?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I remember I was at the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were you given any concrete tasks for the 19th?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: Nothing particular for the 19th except for my own unit concerning its further work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether evacuation was mentioned, the evacuation of the hospital, at the briefing of the 19th?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Veselin Sljivancanin was present at that briefing?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: I think he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Susic, I didn't ask you who the commander of the barracks in Vukovar was.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN SUSIC
utterances.text: The commander of the barracks in Vukovar was Major Branislav Lukic, commander of the 2nd Assault Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
